title: Does Compulsory School Attendance Affect Schooling and Earnings?
research_question: Does additional schooling raise individual earnings? Specifically, what is the causal return to an extra year of education on subsequent labor market earnings, separate from any correlation driven by ability or family background?
data_description: The analysis draws on U.S. Census data, primarily the 1970 and 1980 Public Use Microdata Samples, covering large cohorts of men born between roughly 1930 and 1959. Key variables include years of completed schooling, weekly and annual earnings (log wages), quarter of birth, year of birth, state of birth, race, and other demographics. The unit of observation is the individual worker. Sample sizes run into the hundreds of thousands, allowing precise estimation within narrow birth-cohort cells. Outcomes are examined separately by decade-of-birth cohorts (e.g., men born 1920-29, 1930-39, 1940-49). Auxiliary tabulations link quarter of birth to high school graduation rates and average years of schooling at the cohort level.
institutional_context: U.S. compulsory schooling laws typically require children to remain enrolled until they reach a specified age, often 16 or 17, depending on the state and era. Children, however, begin school in the calendar year they turn six, so a child's age at school entry depends on quarter of birth. As a result, students born early in the calendar year start school at an older age and reach the legal dropout age after completing fewer years of schooling than students born later in the year. Pupils who wish to leave school as soon as legally permitted therefore accumulate different amounts of education depending solely on their birth quarter. This interaction between birth timing and statutory attendance requirements generates exogenous variation in completed schooling that is unrelated to family background or innate ability.
